citations.quote: | A-ST20-GUN-FRC / A-ST30-GUN-FRC | gun force not reached (weld cells) | Often the first sign of low supply air at the cells; see Section 6.2 |

When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows. The weld cells see their regulated gun air fall shortly after; gun force alarms follow, and when gun air reaches each cell's own low limit (see the weld cell manual) the supply-air interlock stops that cell.
A fall in gun air pressure at ST20 and ST30 at the same time, after the header pressure has fallen, places the cause in the air supply, not in the weld cells.

Shortly after header pressure declines, downstream air to the weld guns drops below the 5.6 bar regulator setting. Gun force alarms follow, and once gun pressure falls to the internal low limit of ST20 or ST30, the supply-air interlock halts cell operation.

citations.quote: A narrow bead with normal flow and pressure points to the nozzle or the bead program; a narrow bead with low flow points to the pump supply (see Section 6.2).

Outlet pressure (`pump_pressure_bar`) starts to pulse at the pump stroke rate (0.15 Hz, one stroke about every 6.7 s) and its mean falls. Flow (`flow_rate_ccm`) drops below its normal range of 270 to 330 cc/min. Motor current falls slightly and becomes unsteady because the pump moves less material.
Pressure pulsing at the stroke rate together with falling flow means the pump is not filling on each stroke: a starved inlet or cavitation, not a blocked nozzle.
A blocked nozzle raises outlet pressure and lowers flow; a starved inlet lowers both pressure and flow.

citations.quote: When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows. The weld cells see their regulated gun air fall shortly after; gun force alarms follow, and when gun air reaches each cell's own low limit (see the weld cell manual) the supply-air interlock stops that cell. A leak is often audible as a hiss at the leak point.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.
A fall in gun air pressure at ST20 and ST30 at the same time, after the header pressure has fallen, places the cause in the air supply, not in the weld cells.

citations.quote: | S-ST20-WLD-FLT / S-ST30-WLD-FLT | repeated weld faults, cell stopped | Several weld faults in a row; see Section 6.7 and Section 6.2 |

Typical signature. Weld quality alarms and a growing scatter in tip resistance at ST20 that start soon after a product changeover, with normal tip dressing records, often come from parts formed out of tolerance at the ST10 press.
Check the ST10 press main pressure against the recipe setpoint for the new model (see Table 3-3 of AM-PH-01 (Hydraulic Press and Power Unit)) before changing any weld schedule.

If tip resistance rises at one weld cell only, the tips or the tip dresser at that cell are the cause; if weld faults start at ST20 right after a press changeover, check the parts first (see Section 6.7).

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.
A fall in gun air pressure at ST20 and ST30 at the same time, after the header pressure has fallen, places the cause in the air supply, not in the weld cells.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |

citations.quote: | A-ST20-TIPR-HI | ST20 Weld cell A: tip resistance high | `tip_resistance_mohm` above 0.185 mOhm; alarm: the station keeps running |

Tip resistance (`tip_resistance_mohm`) climbs steadily over hours from about 0.15 mOhm towards the 0.185 mOhm alarm limit as the tip faces pick up coating material and oxide (which raises contact resistance) and lose their shape, while the current stepper raises weld current (`weld_current_ka`) to compensate.
Tip resistance that rises in a straight line over several hours, together with a stepping weld current, is the signature of electrode tip wear, not of a controller fault.

citations.quote: Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. Above 66 degC the drive derates its speed, adding about 0.8 s to the cycle for every degree above that point, so the cell cycle time rises and stations downstream are starved. The 72 degC alarm comes before the 80 degC trip. A failing cabinet fan is often audible before the trip.
On ST30, check coolant flow first: a servo temperature rise that follows a fall in coolant flow is a cooling-circuit problem (see Section 6.4), not a drive problem.
A servo temperature rise with normal coolant flow and a cabinet fan that is noisy, slow or stopped points to the cabinet cooling fan or a clogged cabinet filter.

| Trip S-ST20-SRV-OT or S-ST30-SRV-OT at 80 degC | Sustained overheating not corrected at the alarm stage | Check coolant flow (ST30), the cabinet fan and the gun mechanics for binding | Let the drive cool; restart only after the cause is found |

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.
A fall in gun air pressure at ST20 and ST30 at the same time, after the header pressure has fallen, places the cause in the air supply, not in the weld cells.

A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |
| A-UTAIR-HDR-LO | Plant air compressor and header: header pressure low | `header_pressure_bar` below 5.6 bar; alarm: the station keeps running |

citations.quote: Regulated gun air (`air_pressure_bar`) normally sits at 5.6 bar within 5.3 to 5.9 bar. Below 5 bar the cell raises a low-air alarm; at 4.6 bar the supply-air interlock stops the cell. Gun force alarms (A-ST20-GUN-FRC, A-ST30-GUN-FRC) can appear as the air falls.

When gun air pressure falls at ST20 and ST30 together, the cause is upstream in the plant air supply; check the header pressure (see Section 6.2 of AM-CA-01 (Plant Air System and Utilities)) before working on either cell.
When gun air falls at one cell only, check that cell's filter-regulator, drop-leg ball valve and quick couplings.
| Gun air low at both ST20 and ST30 | Plant air header pressure low (leak or compressor problem) | Check `header_pressure_bar` on UT-AIR | Follow the plant air and utilities manual, Section 6 |

citation.quote: Servo-gun drive temperature (`servo_temp_c`) rises above its normal range of 35 to 65 degC. claims.text: The manual indicates that a servo temperature rise occurring alongside normal coolant flow typically originates from a cabinet fan failure or clogged filter.

claims.text: A coolant flow blockage could cause the servo to overheat, but the telemetry shows perfectly normal coolant flow rates leading up to the trip.

When gun air pressure falls at ST20 and ST30 together, the cause is upstream in the plant air supply; check the header pressure (see Section 6.2 of AM-CA-01 (Plant Air System and Utilities)) before working on either cell.
When gun air falls at one cell only, check that cell's filter-regulator, drop-leg ball valve and quick couplings.

citations.quote: In normal service the compressor loads at 6.2 bar and unloads at 7.3 bar, so header pressure (`header_pressure_bar`) saw-tooths inside its normal range of 6 to 7.5 bar and motor current (`compressor_current_a`) switches between about 92 A loaded and about 38 A unloaded, a load/unload cycle of roughly 2 minutes. A leak first shows as a longer loaded time: average motor current rises while header pressure still recovers. When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.
A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |
| A-UTAIR-HDR-LO | Plant air compressor and header: header pressure low | `header_pressure_bar` below 5.6 bar; alarm: the station keeps running |

citations.quote: Drive-end bearing vibration (`vibration_rms_mms`) rises out of its normal range of 0.8 to 2.8 mm/s, slowly at first and then faster. The one-second RMS trend carries a ripple at the pulley rotation frequency (about 0.255 Hz at 12 m/min, one turn every 3.9 s). Bearing temperature (`bearing_temp_c`) follows some minutes later; motor current rises slightly and chain speed sags.
Vibration that grows in an accelerating curve, with a ripple at the pulley rotation frequency and a delayed rise in bearing temperature, indicates a drive-end bearing defect.

| `vibration_rms_mms` above 2.8 mm/s and accelerating, ripple at 1x pulley rotation | Drive-end bearing defect (race or rolling element damage) | Spectrum of a high-rate snapshot; listen with a stethoscope; check the grease condition | Plan a bearing replacement; reduce speed only under change control; replace at the next stop |

| Vibration high, steady, started after chain or sprocket work | Shaft misalignment or loose bearing housing bolts | Check the housing bolt torque and the shaft alignment | Re-torque the bolts; realign the shaft |
